claims.text: The target material is a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with density below 6 g/cm3.
The as-cast or as-sintered alloy initially has a non-equilibrium metastable microstructure containing solid solutions and intermetallics.
The initial microstructure contains Mg-enriched metastable domains.
Heating or reactive environmental exposure causes stable intermetallic phases to precipitate from the metastable Mg-enriched domains.
The stable intermetallic precipitates preferentially nucleate and grow at grain boundaries.
Intermetallic precipitation produces local redistribution of Mg and other passivating elements near grain boundaries.
Elemental partitioning can deplete Mg from the remaining matrix.
Local elemental chemistry and elemental oxygen reactivity govern oxide nucleation, speciation, and growth.
Redistribution of passivating elements can change the surface oxide from a more reactive layer to a more protective layer, or vice versa.
Ti- and Zn-containing matrices with distributed intermetallics can promote protective surface-film formation and corrosion passivation in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys.
Microstructural evolution will produce progressively more protective oxide scales during high-temperature exposure.
Microstructural evolution will improve oxidation resistance relative to the as-processed state.
Microstructural evolution will modify solution-corrosion pathways and produce region-specific corrosion improvements relative to the as-processed state.
The initial material has moderate corrosion resistance and oxidation stability because Mg-rich metastable domains are incompletely passivated.
The mechanism applies to alloys with distinct metastable Mg-containing phases produced by rapid solidification or powder consolidation.
The proposed transformation can be induced by isothermal holds from 300 to 600 °C under oxidizing or corrosive conditions below incipient melting.
Time-resolved diffraction, microscopy, atom-probe analysis, electrochemical impedance, and oxide characterization can be used to test the proposed transformation–passivation relationship.
The hypothesis is falsified if no new grain-boundary intermetallics form, or if phase transformation occurs without a corresponding change in oxide or passivation behavior.
